title: HTML, CSS & JavaScript
description: Master modern web development from zero. Build layouts, style pages, and write interactive JavaScript code.

modules.title: HTML Foundations & Structure
modules.description: Learn the essential tags and layout building blocks of web pages

content.explanation: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) defines the structure of every webpage. Headings range from <h1> to <h6>, with <h1> being the most important heading on a page.

examples.title: Primary Heading
examples.explanation: Defines the main title of your web page.

examples.title: Secondary Heading
examples.explanation: Defines a sub-heading or section title.

key_points: HTML elements are defined using tags with opening <tag> and closing </tag>
<h1> is used for the main topic of the document
Keep only one <h1> per page for optimal structure and SEO

challenge.title: Create your first <h1> heading
challenge.description: Create an <h1> heading tag containing the text 'Hello World'.

quiz.question: What does HTML stand for?
quiz.explanation: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language, the standard format for web pages.

quiz.question: Which heading tag represents the highest level heading in HTML?
quiz.explanation: <h1> represents the primary level-1 heading.

content.explanation:
The

tag defines a paragraph of text. Browsers automatically add a margin before and after each paragraph element.

examples.title: Standard Paragraph
examples.code: This is a paragraph explaining web technologies.
examples.explanation: Creates a distinct block of text with default vertical spacing.

key_points:
Use

tags for blocks of text and sentences
White spaces and line breaks inside HTML are collapsed unless wrapped in appropriate tags

challenge.title: Write a Paragraph Tag
challenge.description:
Create a

element with the text 'Learning code is fun'.

quiz.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a standard paragraph?
quiz.explanation: is the standard HTML element for paragraphs.

content.explanation: Hyperlinks are created with the <a> (anchor) tag. The 'href' attribute specifies the destination URL of the link.

examples.title: Anchor Link Example
examples.explanation: Creates a clickable link to Google.

key_points: <a> stands for anchor
The href attribute is mandatory for functional links
Text between and is the clickable label

challenge.title: Create a Clickable Link
challenge.description: Create an <a> tag with an href attribute containing 'Visit'.

quiz.question: Which attribute holds the URL address in an HTML link?
quiz.explanation: The 'href' (hypertext reference) attribute specifies the target URL.

content.explanation: The <button> element represents a clickable button used to submit forms, trigger dialogs, or initiate actions in modern web apps.

examples.title: Action Button
examples.explanation: A clickable button with text.

key_points: Buttons can be styled extensively with CSS
Can be connected to JavaScript event listeners

challenge.title: Create a Get Started Button
challenge.description: Create a <button> tag with the text 'Get Started'.

quiz.question: Which element is used for clickable actions in HTML5?
quiz.explanation: <button> is the standard element for user actions.

content.explanation:
Lists organize related items using
    (unordered) or
      (ordered), with each item wrapped in
    1. . Images are embedded with the self-closing tag, which requires a 'src' attribute and an 'alt' attribute for accessibility.

examples.title: Unordered List
examples.explanation: Displays a bulleted list of three items.

examples.title: Image Tag
examples.explanation: Embeds an image with a descriptive alt attribute.

key_points: <ul> creates bullet points, <ol> creates numbered lists
Every list item goes inside an <li> tag
is self-closing with no closing tag
The 'alt' attribute is required for accessibility and SEO

challenge.title: Build a List of Skills
challenge.description: Create an unordered list <ul> with at least one <li> item containing the word 'HTML'.

rules.description: Must have at least one <li> element

quiz.question: Which attribute is required on an tag for accessibility?
quiz.explanation: The 'alt' attribute describes the image for screen readers and SEO.

quiz.question: Which tag creates a numbered list?
quiz.explanation: <ol> stands for ordered list and produces numbered items.

content.explanation: Semantic elements clearly describe their meaning to both the browser and the developer, instead of using generic <div> for everything. Tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer> describe the role of each part of the page.

examples.title: Semantic Page Skeleton
examples.explanation: Structures a page using meaningful, self-describing tags instead of generic divs.

key_points: Semantic tags improve accessibility and SEO
<main> should contain the primary content of the page, and appear once
<article> represents self-contained content, <section> groups related content

challenge.title: Build a Semantic Layout
challenge.description: Create a page skeleton using <header>, <main>, and <footer> tags.

quiz.question: Which semantic tag should contain the unique main content of a page?
quiz.explanation: <main> identifies the dominant, unique content of the document body.

modules.title: HTML Forms & Accessibility
modules.description: Collect user input with forms and build pages that everyone can use

content.explanation: The <form> element wraps controls that collect user input. The most common control is <input>, whose 'type' attribute determines what kind of data it accepts, such as 'text' for plain text.

examples.title: Simple Text Input
examples.explanation: Creates a form with a single text field.

key_points: <form> groups related input controls together
input type="text" accepts single-line free text
The 'placeholder' attribute shows hint text inside an empty field
The 'name' attribute identifies the field when the form is submitted

challenge.title: Create a Text Input Form
challenge.description: Create a <form> containing an <input> of type 'text'.

rules.description: Input must have a type attribute

quiz.question: Which HTML element wraps input controls for collecting user data?
quiz.explanation: <form> groups and submits related input controls.

content.explanation: The <label> element gives an input a descriptive, clickable name. Connecting a label to its input with a matching 'for' attribute and input 'id' makes forms usable for screen readers and lets users click the label to focus the field.

examples.title: Labeled Input
examples.explanation: The label's 'for' attribute matches the input's 'id', linking them together.

key_points: 'for' on <label> must match the 'id' on the related <input>
Labels improve accessibility for screen reader users
Clicking a properly linked label focuses its input

challenge.title: Link a Label to an Input
challenge.description: Create a <label for="email"> and an <input id="email"> that are properly linked.

rules.description: Label must have a for attribute
Input must have an id attribute

hints: Set id="email" on the matching input

quiz.question: Which attribute links a <label> to its <input>?
quiz.explanation: A label's 'for' attribute must match the input's 'id' attribute.

content.explanation: HTML5 offers many input types beyond plain text, including 'email', 'password', 'number', and 'checkbox'. Browsers automatically validate and style these differently — for example, 'email' checks for a valid email format.

examples.title: Password and Checkbox
examples.explanation: A masked password field and a togglable checkbox.

key_points: type="email" validates basic email format automatically
type="password" masks entered characters
type="checkbox" allows toggling a boolean option
type="number" restricts input to numeric values

challenge.title: Create a Password Field
challenge.description: Create an <input> of type 'password' with name 'pw'.

quiz.question: Which input type automatically masks the characters typed?
quiz.explanation: type="password" hides typed characters behind dots or asterisks.

content.explanation: The <select> element creates a dropdown list of <option> elements. The <textarea> element provides a resizable multi-line text box, unlike the single-line <input type="text">.

examples.title: Dropdown Menu
examples.explanation: Lets the user pick one plan from a list.

key_points: <select> wraps one or more <option> elements
Each <option> has a 'value' sent when the form is submitted
<textarea> is used for longer, multi-line text like comments

challenge.title: Build a Dropdown
challenge.description: Create a <select> with at least two <option> elements.

quiz.question: Which element creates a multi-line text input?
quiz.explanation: <textarea> provides a resizable, multi-line text box.

content.explanation: A form is submitted with an <input type="submit"> or a <button type="submit">. By default, submitting a form reloads the page and sends its data to the URL in the form's 'action' attribute.

examples.title: Submit Button
examples.explanation: Submits the form data to '/signup' when the button is clicked.

key_points: type="submit" on a button triggers form submission
The 'action' attribute defines where form data is sent
The 'method' attribute (GET or POST) defines how data is sent

challenge.title: Add a Submit Button
challenge.description: Add a <button type="submit"> inside a <form>.

quiz.question: Which form attribute defines where the data is sent on submit?
quiz.explanation: The 'action' attribute specifies the URL that receives the submitted form data.

content.explanation: Accessibility (a11y) means building pages usable by everyone, including people using screen readers or keyboards only. ARIA attributes like 'aria-label' provide extra context when visible text isn't enough, and semantic HTML should always be preferred over ARIA when possible.

examples.title: Accessible Icon Button
examples.explanation: Gives a screen reader a meaningful label for a button with only a symbol as its visible text.

key_points: Prefer native semantic elements before reaching for ARIA
'aria-label' provides an accessible name when visible text is missing or unclear
All interactive elements should be reachable and usable via keyboard

challenge.title: Add an Accessible Label
challenge.description: Create a <button> with an aria-label attribute.

quiz.question: What should be preferred over ARIA attributes whenever possible?
quiz.explanation: Native semantic HTML elements already carry accessibility meaning and should be preferred over ARIA patches.

modules.title: CSS Fundamentals: Colors, Typography & Selectors
modules.description: Bring web pages to life with colors, fonts, and ways to target elements

content.explanation: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls colors, layout, and presentation. You can change text color using the 'color' property and backgrounds using 'background-color'.

examples.title: Inline Color Style
examples.explanation: Applies a custom hex color directly to an element.

key_points: The style attribute allows adding CSS rules directly
'color' controls text color, 'background-color' sets the background
Hex codes like #6366f1 or names like 'red' can be used

challenge.title: Style an Element with Color
challenge.description: Create an <h2> tag with a style attribute specifying color.

quiz.question: Which CSS property is used to set the text color?
quiz.explanation: The 'color' property defines the foreground text color.

content.explanation: Typography properties control how text looks: 'font-size' sets its size, 'font-weight' sets boldness, and 'font-family' chooses the typeface. A 'font-family' should list a fallback stack in case the first font isn't available.

examples.title: Styled Text
examples.code: Bold text
examples.explanation: Sets a larger, bold paragraph using Arial with a sans-serif fallback.

key_points: font-size is commonly set in px or rem
font-weight: bold (or 700) makes text heavier
Always include a generic fallback like sans-serif or serif

challenge.title: Style Text with Typography
challenge.description:
Create a

with a style attribute that includes 'font-size'.

quiz.question: Which CSS property controls how thick or bold text appears?
quiz.explanation: 'font-weight' controls the thickness of the font, e.g. normal or bold.

content.explanation: Instead of inline styles, CSS is usually applied through reusable classes defined with a dot ('.') inside a <style> block or external stylesheet, keeping styling separate from content.

examples.title: Class Selector
examples.explanation: Defines a reusable '.highlight' class and applies it to a paragraph.

key_points: Classes are reusable across many elements: class="name"
In CSS, classes are selected with a dot: .name { ... }
Separating style from HTML markup keeps code easier to maintain

challenge.title: Apply a CSS Class
challenge.description: Create a

rules.description: Must define and use a class named 'highlight'
An element must use the class attribute

quiz.question: Which symbol is used to select a CSS class?
quiz.explanation: A dot (.) prefixes class selectors in CSS.

content.explanation: An 'id' uniquely identifies a single element on a page and is selected in CSS with a hash ('#'). ID selectors are more 'specific' than class selectors, meaning their rules override conflicting class rules when both apply.

examples.title: ID Selector
examples.explanation: Targets the single element with id 'main-title' and colors it crimson.

key_points: IDs must be unique per page: id="name"
CSS selects IDs with a hash: #name { ... }
ID rules win over class rules of equal weight due to higher specificity

challenge.title: Style an Element by ID
challenge.description: Create a <style> block targeting #main-title, and an <h1 id="main-title">.

rules.description: An element must use the id attribute

quiz.question: Between a class rule and an ID rule targeting the same element, which one wins?
options: The ID rule, due to higher specificity
Whichever is written last, regardless of type
quiz.explanation: ID selectors carry higher specificity than class selectors in CSS.

content.explanation: 'text-align' controls the horizontal alignment of text inside its container (left, center, right, or justify). 'text-decoration' adds or removes effects like underlines, which is often used to remove the default underline from links.

examples.title: Centered Heading
examples.explanation: Centers the heading text horizontally within its container.

key_points: text-align: center centers text horizontally
text-decoration: none removes underlines, often used on links
text-align only affects inline/text content, not the box position itself

challenge.title: Center a Heading
challenge.description: Create an <h2> with style="text-align: center;".

quiz.question: Which CSS property removes the underline from a link?
quiz.explanation: 'text-decoration: none' removes underlines and other decorations from text.

content.explanation: Beyond system fonts, custom web fonts (like Google Fonts) can be linked into a page with a <link> tag in the <head>, then applied with 'font-family' just like any other font.

examples.title: Linking a Web Font
examples.explanation: Loads the Roboto font and applies it to a paragraph.

key_points: Custom fonts are typically loaded via a <link> tag in <head>
Always keep a generic fallback like sans-serif after a custom font name
Too many custom fonts can slow down page load time

challenge.title: Apply a Custom Font Family
challenge.description:
Create a

with style="font-family: 'Roboto', sans-serif;".

quiz.question: Where is a Google Font typically linked into an HTML page?
options: It cannot be linked, only downloaded
quiz.explanation: A <link> tag referencing the font stylesheet is placed in the <head> so it loads before content renders.

modules.title: CSS Box Model & Spacing
modules.description: Understand how every element is a box, and control spacing between them

lessons.title: The Box Model: Padding, Margin & Border

content.explanation: Every HTML element is a rectangular box made of four parts: content, padding, border, and margin. Padding is space inside the border, margin is space outside the border, and the border wraps the padding and content.

examples.title: Box Model Spacing
examples.explanation: Adds inner spacing, outer spacing, and a visible border to a div.

key_points: padding = space inside the border, around the content
margin = space outside the border, between elements
border adds a visible line around the padding and content

challenge.title: Style a Box with Padding
challenge.description: Create a <div> with a style attribute that includes 'padding'.

quiz.question: Which box model property adds space OUTSIDE an element's border?
quiz.explanation: Margin creates space outside the border, separating elements from one another.

content.explanation: 'width' and 'height' set an element's content size. By default, padding and border add to that size, but 'box-sizing: border-box' makes padding and border count inside the declared width and height, which is easier to reason about.

examples.title: Border-Box Sizing
examples.explanation: The div stays exactly 200px wide total, because padding is included rather than added.

key_points: Default box-sizing is 'content-box': padding/border add extra width
'border-box' includes padding and border inside the declared width/height
Many developers set box-sizing: border-box globally for predictability

challenge.title: Set a Fixed Width Box
challenge.description: Create a <div> with style including both 'width' and 'box-sizing: border-box'.

quiz.question: What does 'box-sizing: border-box' change about width calculation?
options: Padding and border are included inside the declared width
quiz.explanation: With border-box, padding and border no longer add extra size beyond the declared width/height.

content.explanation: The 'display' property determines how an element behaves in the layout. Block elements (like <div>) take up the full width and start on a new line; inline elements (like <span>) flow within text and only take up as much width as needed.

examples.title: Inline vs Block
examples.explanation: The span stays inline with surrounding content; the div starts on its own line.

key_points: Block elements stack vertically and fill available width by default
Inline elements sit side-by-side within a line of text
'display: inline-block' combines inline flow with block-like sizing

challenge.title: Set Display to Block
challenge.description: Create a <span> with style="display: block;".
challenge.solution: Now on its own line
hints: Add style="display: block;" to the span

quiz.question: Which display value makes an element start on a new line and fill available width?
quiz.explanation: Block-level elements stack vertically and take up the full available width by default.

content.explanation: The 'position' property changes how an element is placed. 'relative' shifts it from its normal position without affecting other elements; 'absolute' removes it from normal flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor.

examples.title: Absolute Badge
examples.code: New
examples.explanation: Positions a 'New' badge in the top-right corner of its relatively positioned parent.

key_points: position: relative keeps the element in flow but allows offsetting it
position: absolute positions relative to the nearest positioned ancestor
top/right/bottom/left set the offset once position is not 'static'

challenge.title: Create an Absolutely Positioned Badge
challenge.description: Create a <div style="position: relative;"> containing a <span style="position: absolute;">.
challenge.solution: New

quiz.question: An absolutely positioned element is placed relative to what?
quiz.explanation: An absolutely positioned element positions itself relative to the nearest ancestor that has a non-static position.

content.explanation: When content is bigger than its container, the 'overflow' property decides what happens: 'visible' (default, spills out), 'hidden' (clipped), or 'scroll'/'auto' (adds scrollbars).

examples.title: Scrollable Box
examples.code: Long content that needs scrolling...
examples.explanation: Adds a scrollbar automatically if the content exceeds the fixed height.

key_points: overflow: hidden clips content that doesn't fit
overflow: auto shows a scrollbar only when needed
overflow: scroll always shows scrollbars, even if not needed

challenge.title: Make a Scrollable Box
challenge.description: Create a <div> with style including 'overflow: auto' and a fixed 'height'.

quiz.question: Which overflow value clips overflowing content without adding a scrollbar?
quiz.explanation: 'hidden' clips any content that exceeds the element's box, with no scrollbar shown.

content.explanation: CSS sizes can be absolute (like 'px', a fixed pixel value) or relative. '%' is relative to the parent's size, 'em' is relative to the current element's font size, and 'rem' is relative to the root (<html>) font size, making it predictable across a whole page.

examples.title: Relative Sizing
examples.explanation: Sets font size relative to the root, and width relative to the parent container.

key_points: px is a fixed, absolute unit
% sizes relative to the parent element
rem sizes relative to the root <html> font-size, consistent site-wide

challenge.title: Use rem Units
challenge.description:
Create a

with style="font-size: 1.5rem;".

quiz.question: The 'rem' unit is relative to what?
quiz.explanation: 'rem' stands for root em, and is always relative to the <html> element's font size.

modules.title: Modern CSS Layout: Flexbox & Grid
modules.description: Arrange elements on the page using the two pillars of modern CSS layout

content.explanation: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system for arranging items in a row or column. Setting 'display: flex' on a container turns its direct children into flex items that can be aligned and distributed with properties like 'justify-content'.

examples.title: Flex Container
examples.explanation: Places two boxes in a row with space distributed between them.

key_points: display: flex turns a container into a flex container
justify-content aligns items along the main axis (horizontal by default)
align-items aligns items along the cross axis (vertical by default)

challenge.title: Create a Flex Container
challenge.description: Create a <div> with style="display: flex;" containing two nested <div> elements.
hints: Set style="display: flex;" on the outer div

quiz.question: Which CSS property turns a container into a flexbox?
quiz.explanation: 'display: flex' activates flexbox layout on the container.

quiz.question: Which flexbox property distributes space along the main axis?
quiz.explanation: 'justify-content' controls alignment and spacing along the main axis.

content.explanation: 'flex-direction' controls whether flex items are laid out in a row (default) or a column. 'flex-wrap: wrap' allows items to move onto a new line instead of shrinking to fit a single row.

examples.title: Column Layout
examples.explanation: Stacks flex items vertically instead of horizontally.

key_points: flex-direction: row (default) lays items left to right
flex-direction: column stacks items top to bottom
flex-wrap: wrap lets items flow onto multiple lines

challenge.title: Stack Items in a Column
challenge.description: Create a flex container with style including 'flex-direction: column'.
hints: Add flex-direction: column; alongside display: flex;

quiz.question: Which value of flex-direction stacks items vertically?
quiz.explanation: flex-direction: column arranges flex items top to bottom.

lessons.title: Aligning Items on the Cross Axis

content.explanation: 'align-items' controls how flex items are aligned perpendicular to the main axis (vertically, in a row layout). Common values are 'flex-start', 'center', and 'flex-end', with 'center' being especially useful for vertical centering.

examples.title: Vertically Centered Items
examples.explanation: Vertically centers the child inside a 150px-tall flex container.

key_points: align-items: center vertically centers items in a row layout
align-items works on the cross axis, perpendicular to flex-direction
Combining justify-content: center and align-items: center centers content both ways

challenge.title: Vertically Center a Flex Item
challenge.description: Create a flex container with style including 'align-items: center'.
hints: Add align-items: center; to your flex container

quiz.question: In a default row flexbox, what axis does 'align-items' control?
options: It has no effect in a row layout
quiz.explanation: align-items controls alignment along the cross axis, which is vertical when flex-direction is row.

content.explanation: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system that arranges elements into rows and columns simultaneously. Setting 'display: grid' with 'grid-template-columns' defines how many columns the layout has and how wide they are.

examples.title: Simple Grid
examples.explanation: Creates a two-column grid with equal-width columns.

key_points: display: grid activates grid layout
grid-template-columns defines column sizes, e.g. '1fr 1fr' for two equal columns
'fr' stands for fractional unit, a share of available space

challenge.title: Build a Two-Column Grid
challenge.description: Create a <div> using display: grid and grid-template-columns to make two columns.

quiz.question: What does the 'fr' unit represent in CSS Grid?
quiz.explanation: 'fr' is a fractional unit representing a share of the remaining space in the grid.

content.explanation: 'gap' adds consistent spacing between grid (or flex) items without needing margins on each one. 'grid-template-rows' works like grid-template-columns but defines the height of each row instead.

examples.title: Grid with Gap
examples.explanation: Adds 16px of spacing between every grid cell.

key_points: gap adds space between grid/flex items in one property
grid-template-rows defines the height of each row
gap replaces the need for manual margins between grid items

challenge.title: Add Spacing to a Grid
challenge.description: Create a grid container with style including both 'display: grid' and 'gap'.
hints: Add gap: 16px; to your grid container

quiz.question: What does the 'gap' property control in a grid layout?
quiz.explanation: 'gap' sets consistent spacing between rows and columns of grid (or flex) items.

content.explanation: Flexbox and Grid solve different problems. Flexbox excels at one-dimensional layouts (a single row or column, like a navbar), while Grid excels at two-dimensional layouts (rows AND columns together, like a page template or photo gallery). They can also be combined.

examples.title: Navbar with Flexbox
examples.explanation: A simple one-dimensional navbar is a classic flexbox use case.

key_points: Use Flexbox for one-dimensional arrangements: a single row or column
Use Grid for two-dimensional arrangements: rows and columns together
A whole page layout often uses Grid for structure and Flexbox inside components

challenge.title: Build a Flexbox Navbar
challenge.description: Create a <nav> with style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between;" containing two child elements.
hints: Use display: flex; justify-content: space-between; on the nav

quiz.question: Which layout system is best suited for a simple one-dimensional navbar?
quiz.explanation: Flexbox is ideal for one-dimensional layouts like a row of navbar items.

modules.title: Responsive Design & Animations
modules.description: Make pages adapt to any screen size and bring interfaces to life with motion

content.explanation: Media queries apply CSS rules only when certain conditions are met, most commonly screen width. '@media (max-width: 600px) { ... }' applies its rules only on screens 600px wide or narrower, enabling responsive, mobile-friendly designs.

examples.title: Mobile Breakpoint
examples.explanation: Changes the box's background color only when the viewport is 600px wide or less.

key_points: @media (max-width: Npx) targets screens N pixels wide or smaller
Media queries are the foundation of responsive web design
Common breakpoints target phones, tablets, and desktops

challenge.title: Write a Media Query
challenge.description: Create a <style> block with an @media (max-width: 600px) rule.

quiz.question: What does '@media (max-width: 600px)' target?
quiz.explanation: max-width in a media query matches viewports at or below that width.

content.explanation: Setting 'max-width: 100%' on an image prevents it from overflowing its container on small screens, while letting it display at full size on larger ones. This single rule is one of the most common responsive design techniques.

examples.title: Fluid Image
examples.explanation: The image shrinks to fit its container but never stretches beyond its natural size.

key_points: max-width: 100% prevents images from overflowing their container
height: auto keeps the image's aspect ratio when its width shrinks
This pattern is essential for mobile-friendly pages

challenge.title: Make an Image Responsive
challenge.description: Create an tag with style including 'max-width: 100%'.
hints: Add style="max-width: 100%; height: auto;" to the img

quiz.question: Which style prevents an image from overflowing its container on small screens?
quiz.explanation: max-width: 100% caps the image size at its container's width, shrinking on smaller screens.

content.explanation: Without a viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render pages at a wide desktop-like width and zoom out. Adding '<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">' in the <head> tells the browser to match the page width to the device's actual screen width.

examples.title: Viewport Meta Tag
examples.explanation: Ensures the page renders at the device's real width instead of a zoomed-out desktop layout.

key_points: Without this tag, mobile browsers assume a ~980px wide desktop layout
width=device-width matches the CSS viewport to the device screen width
initial-scale=1 sets the initial zoom level to 100%

challenge.title: Add a Viewport Meta Tag
challenge.description: Create a <meta> tag with name="viewport" and content including 'width=device-width'.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the viewport meta tag?
options: It adds a border to the page
It matches the page's width to the device's actual screen width
It changes the font of the page
quiz.explanation: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers to render the page at the device's real width instead of a zoomed-out layout.

content.explanation: 'transition' smoothly animates a CSS property change over time, instead of it happening instantly. It's commonly combined with ':hover' to create smooth effects when a user moves their mouse over an element.

examples.title: Hover Transition
examples.code:
<style>
button { background-color: royalblue; transition: background-color 0.3s; }
button:hover { background-color: darkblue; }
</style>
examples.explanation: The button's background smoothly fades to a darker blue over 0.3 seconds on hover.

key_points: transition: property duration animates changes to that property
':hover' triggers styles when the mouse is over an element
Common transition durations range from 0.2s to 0.5s for a smooth feel

challenge.title: Add a Hover Transition
challenge.description: Create a <style> block with a button rule that includes 'transition' and a ':hover' rule.
challenge.solution:
<style>
button { background-color: royalblue; transition: background-color 0.3s; }
button:hover { background-color: darkblue; }
</style>
<button>Hover me</button>
hints: Add transition: background-color 0.3s; to the button rule

quiz.question: Which CSS property animates a smooth change between two style states?
quiz.explanation: 'transition' smoothly animates a property's change from one value to another over a set duration.

content.explanation: 'transform' changes an element's shape or position visually, without affecting the layout of surrounding elements. Common functions include 'scale()' to resize, 'rotate()' to spin, and 'translate()' to move.

examples.title: Scale on Hover
examples.explanation: Enlarges the card slightly to 105% of its size when hovered.

key_points: transform: scale(1.05) enlarges an element to 105% of its size
transform: rotate(45deg) rotates an element by 45 degrees
transform doesn't affect the space other elements take up, unlike changing width/height directly

challenge.title: Scale an Element on Hover
challenge.description: Create a <style> block with a '.card:hover' rule that uses 'transform: scale'.

quiz.question: Which transform function resizes an element?
quiz.explanation: scale() resizes an element visually, e.g. scale(1.05) makes it 5% larger.

content.explanation: '@keyframes' defines a multi-step animation sequence by naming stages from 0% to 100%. An element then runs that animation using the 'animation' property, specifying the keyframe name and duration.

examples.title: Fade In Animation
examples.code:
<style>
@keyframes fadeIn {
  from { opacity: 0; }
  to { opacity: 1; }
}
.box { animation: fadeIn 1s; }
</style>
examples.explanation: Fades an element from invisible to fully visible over 1 second.

key_points: @keyframes name { ... } defines the animation's stages
'from'/'to' or percentages (0%, 50%, 100%) mark animation stages
The 'animation' property applies a keyframe animation with a duration

challenge.title: Create a Fade-In Animation
challenge.description: Create a <style> block with an @keyframes fadeIn rule and apply it with the 'animation' property.
challenge.solution: Fading in
hints: Apply it with animation: fadeIn 1s; on the .box class

quiz.question: Which rule defines the stages of a custom CSS animation?
quiz.explanation: @keyframes defines the sequence of styles an animation moves through over time.

modules.title: JavaScript Fundamentals
modules.description: Add dynamic behavior, variables, and logic to web applications

content.explanation: JavaScript is the programming language of the web. The console.log() method writes messages and debug data to the browser console.

examples.title: Console Log
examples.explanation: Prints text directly to the console.

key_points: console.log is the most widely used debugging tool
Statements typically end with a semicolon (;)
Strings are wrapped in quotes: 'single', "double", or `backticks`

challenge.title: Print to the Console
challenge.description: Write a JavaScript statement that calls console.log with 'Ready to Code'.

quiz.question: Which method is used in JavaScript to print output to the console?
quiz.explanation: console.log() writes output to the browser/node console.

content.explanation: Variables store data for later use. Modern JavaScript uses 'let' for values that can change and 'const' for values that stay constant. The older 'var' keyword is mostly avoided in new code due to scoping issues.

examples.title: Declaring Variables
examples.explanation: Declares a changeable 'score' and a constant 'name'; only 'let' variables can be reassigned.

key_points: 'let' declares a variable that can be reassigned
'const' declares a variable that cannot be reassigned
Variable names are case-sensitive and typically use camelCase

challenge.title: Declare and Log a Variable
challenge.description: Declare a 'let' variable named score set to 10, then log it with console.log.
challenge.starter_code: // Declare your variable and log it

rules.description: Must declare a variable named score using let

quiz.question: Which keyword should be used for a variable that will never be reassigned?
quiz.explanation: 'const' creates a constant binding that cannot be reassigned.

content.explanation: JavaScript has several basic data types: 'string' for text, 'number' for both integers and decimals, 'boolean' for true/false, and 'undefined' for a variable that has no assigned value yet. The 'typeof' operator returns a value's type as text.

examples.title: Checking Types
examples.explanation: typeof reveals the data type of any value.

key_points: JavaScript does not require declaring types explicitly
'typeof value' returns the type as a string, e.g. "number"
Unlike some languages, JS has one 'number' type for both integers and decimals

challenge.title: Check a Value's Type
challenge.description: Write JavaScript that logs the result of typeof 42 using console.log.

quiz.question: What does 'typeof "hello"' return?
quiz.explanation: Text values in JavaScript have the type "string".

content.explanation: Conditional statements let a program make decisions. An 'if' statement runs a code block only when its condition is true, and 'else' provides a fallback. Comparison operators like '>', '<', and '===' produce true/false values used in these conditions.

examples.title: Simple If/Else
examples.explanation: Logs 'Adult' because age (20) is greater than or equal to 18.

key_points: if (condition) { ... } runs code only when the condition is true
else { ... } runs when the if condition is false
=== checks strict equality (value AND type)

challenge.title: Write an If/Else Statement
challenge.description: Write an if/else statement that logs 'Adult' if a variable age is 18 or greater, otherwise logs 'Minor'.
challenge.starter_code:
let age = 20;
// Write your if/else statement below

quiz.question: Which operator checks strict equality in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: '===' compares both value and type without type coercion.

content.explanation: Logical operators combine multiple conditions. '&&' (AND) is true only when both sides are true, while '||' (OR) is true when at least one side is true. These are commonly used inside 'if' statements to check multiple conditions at once.

examples.title: Combining Conditions
examples.explanation: Only allows entry when both conditions (age and ticket) are true.

key_points: && requires both conditions to be true
|| requires at least one condition to be true
! negates a boolean, turning true into false and vice versa

challenge.title: Combine Two Conditions
challenge.description: Write an if statement that uses '&&' to check two boolean conditions.

quiz.question: When is 'a && b' true?
options: When either a or b is true
Only when both a and b are true
quiz.explanation: The logical AND (&&) operator only evaluates to true when both operands are true.

content.explanation: Template literals, written with backticks (`), let you embed variables directly inside strings using ${...} syntax, instead of manually joining strings with the '+' operator. They also support multi-line strings naturally.

examples.title: String Interpolation
examples.explanation: Embeds the 'name' variable directly inside the string.

key_points: Template literals use backticks (`) instead of quotes
${expression} embeds a variable or expression inside the string
Template literals can span multiple lines without special characters

challenge.title: Use a Template Literal
challenge.description: Write JavaScript that uses a template literal with ${} to log a greeting including a name variable.
challenge.starter_code:
let name = "Alex";
// Log a greeting using a template literal

rules.description: Must use ${name} inside a template literal

quiz.question: Which character is used to create a template literal in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Template literals are delimited by backticks and support ${} interpolation.

modules.title: JavaScript Functions, Arrays & Objects
modules.description: Organize logic into reusable functions and work with collections of data

content.explanation: Functions group reusable blocks of code under a name, defined with the 'function' keyword. Once defined, a function can be called multiple times with different inputs, and can return a value using 'return'.

examples.title: Function with Return
examples.explanation: Defines a function that returns the sum of two parameters, then logs the result.

key_points: 'function name(params) { ... }' defines a function
'return' sends a value back to wherever the function was called
A function without 'return' implicitly returns undefined

challenge.title: Write a Function that Returns a Sum
challenge.description: Define a function called add that takes two parameters and returns their sum, then log the result of add(3, 4).

rules.description: Must define a function named add

hints: Use return a + b; inside the function
Call console.log(add(3, 4)); to see the result

quiz.question: What does a JavaScript function return if it has no explicit 'return' statement?
quiz.explanation: Without an explicit return, a JavaScript function returns undefined by default.

content.explanation: Arrow functions are a shorter syntax for writing functions, using '=>' instead of the 'function' keyword. They're especially common for short, one-off functions passed as arguments to other functions.

examples.title: Arrow Function Syntax
examples.code:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log(add(3, 4));
examples.explanation: A single-expression arrow function implicitly returns the result, no 'return' keyword needed.

key_points: Arrow functions use (params) => expression syntax
A single expression is implicitly returned without needing 'return'
Arrow functions are often stored in a const variable

challenge.title: Write an Arrow Function
challenge.description: Define an arrow function called add that takes two parameters and returns their sum using => syntax.
challenge.solution:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log(add(3, 4));
hints: Write const add = (a, b) => a + b;

quiz.question: Which symbol defines an arrow function?
quiz.explanation: Arrow functions use the '=>' syntax, e.g. (a, b) => a + b.

content.explanation: An array stores an ordered collection of items in square brackets, separated by commas. Items are accessed by their position (index), starting at 0, and the '.push()' method adds a new item to the end.

examples.title: Creating and Accessing an Array
examples.explanation: Creates an array, logs the first item, and adds a new item to the end.

key_points: Arrays are defined with square brackets: [item1, item2]
Indexing starts at 0, so fruits[0] is the first item
The .push() method adds an item to the end of an array

challenge.title: Create and Modify an Array
challenge.description: Create an array called fruits with 'apple' and 'banana', then use .push() to add 'mango'.

rules.description: Must define an array named fruits

quiz.question: What index does the first item in a JavaScript array have?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript arrays are zero-indexed, so the first item is at index 0.

content.explanation: '.forEach()' runs a function once for every item in an array, useful for side effects like logging. '.map()' also runs a function for every item, but builds and returns a brand new array of the results.

examples.title: Using map
examples.explanation: Creates a new array where every number has been doubled.

key_points: forEach runs a function on each item but returns undefined
map returns a brand new array built from the return values
Both take a callback function as their argument

challenge.title: Double Every Number with map
challenge.description: Use .map() on an array called nums to create a new array where every number is doubled.
challenge.starter_code:
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
// Use map to double every number

quiz.question: What does the .map() array method return?
options: A brand new array of transformed items
quiz.explanation: .map() builds and returns a new array containing the results of calling the function on every item.

content.explanation: An object stores data as key-value pairs in curly braces. Values are accessed by their key rather than a numeric position, making objects ideal for structured, labeled data like a user's profile.

examples.title: Creating and Accessing an Object
examples.explanation: Creates an object with two keys and logs the value for 'name'.

key_points: Objects use curly braces: { key: value }
Values are accessed with dot notation: obj.key, or brackets: obj['key']
Keys are usually strings and should be unique within the object

challenge.description: Create an object called user with a key 'name' set to 'Alex', then log user.name.

rules.description: Must define an object named user

quiz.question: How is a value typically retrieved from a JavaScript object?
options: Using dot notation with its key
quiz.explanation: Object values are retrieved using dot notation (obj.key) or bracket notation (obj['key']).

content.explanation: Real-world data is often modeled as an array of objects — for example, a list of users, each with their own name and age. Combining arrays and objects lets you represent structured collections, which can then be looped over with forEach or map.

examples.title: Looping an Array of Objects
examples.explanation: Logs the name of every user in the array.

key_points: An array of objects models a list of structured records
Access each object's properties with dot notation inside the loop
This pattern is extremely common in real applications (e.g. API data)

quiz.question: What real-world data pattern does 'an array of objects' typically represent?
options: A list of structured records, like users or products
quiz.explanation: Arrays of objects are the standard way to represent lists of structured records such as users, products, or API results.

modules.title: DOM Manipulation & Events

content.explanation: The DOM (Document Object Model) represents the HTML page as objects JavaScript can manipulate. 'document.querySelector()' finds the first element matching a CSS selector, allowing scripts to read or change page content.

examples.title: Selecting an Element
examples.explanation: Selects the first <h1> on the page and logs its text.

key_points: document.querySelector('selector') returns the first matching element
'.textContent' reads or sets an element's text
CSS selectors like '#id', '.class', or 'tag' can all be used

quiz.question: Which method selects the first matching element in the DOM?
quiz.explanation: document.querySelector() returns the first element matching a CSS selector.

content.explanation: 'document.querySelectorAll()' returns every element matching a CSS selector, as a NodeList. Unlike querySelector, which returns only the first match, this lets you loop through and act on all matching elements at once.

examples.title: Selecting All Matches
examples.explanation: Selects every element with class 'item' and logs each one's text.

key_points: querySelectorAll returns a NodeList of ALL matching elements
NodeLists support .forEach() just like arrays
Use querySelector for one element, querySelectorAll for many

options: A NodeList of all matching elements
quiz.explanation: querySelectorAll returns a NodeList containing every element that matches the selector.

content.explanation: Once an element is selected, JavaScript can change what it displays by setting '.textContent', or change its appearance by setting properties on '.style', such as '.style.color'.

examples.title: Updating Text and Style
examples.explanation: Changes the box's text and makes it red.

key_points: element.textContent = '...' replaces an element's text
element.style.property = 'value' changes a single CSS property directly
Style property names in JS use camelCase, e.g. backgroundColor

quiz.question: How do you change an element's text color from JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: The .style.color property sets an element's text color directly from JavaScript.

content.explanation: Event listeners let JavaScript respond to user actions like clicks. 'addEventListener' attaches a function that runs whenever the specified event, such as 'click', occurs on an element.

examples.title: Click Listener
examples.explanation: Logs a message every time the button is clicked.

key_points: addEventListener(event, callback) attaches an event handler
'click' is the most common event for buttons and links
The callback function runs each time the event fires

challenge.description: Write JavaScript that selects a button and adds a 'click' event listener that logs 'Clicked!'.

quiz.question: Which method attaches an event handler to an element?
quiz.explanation: addEventListener() registers a function to run when a specified event occurs.

content.explanation: New elements can be created entirely in JavaScript with 'document.createElement()', then added to the page with 'appendChild()'. This lets scripts build page content dynamically instead of only editing what already exists.

examples.title: Creating a New Element
examples.explanation: Creates a new paragraph and adds it to the end of the page body.

key_points: document.createElement('tag') creates a new, unattached element
Setting .textContent gives the new element its content
.appendChild() attaches the new element to a parent in the page

quiz.question: Which method attaches a newly created element to the page?

content.explanation: The 'input' event fires every time a user types into a text field, letting a script react live as the value changes — useful for things like live character counters or search-as-you-type. 'event.target.value' reads the current text.

examples.title: Live Input Tracking
examples.explanation: Logs the input's current text every time the user types a character.

key_points: The 'input' event fires on every keystroke in a text field
event.target refers to the element the event happened on
event.target.value reads the current text of an input field

quiz.explanation: The 'input' event fires immediately after every character is typed or removed.

modules.title: Async JavaScript, APIs & Deployment
modules.description: Fetch real data from the web and put your finished project online

content.explanation: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for representing structured data, closely resembling JS objects and arrays. 'JSON.parse()' converts a JSON string into a real JavaScript object; 'JSON.stringify()' does the reverse.

examples.title: Parsing JSON
examples.explanation: Converts a JSON string into a usable JavaScript object.

key_points: JSON.parse(text) converts a JSON string into a JS object/array
JSON.stringify(obj) converts a JS object/array into a JSON string
Most web APIs send and receive data in JSON format

challenge.title: Parse a JSON String
challenge.description: Use JSON.parse() to convert a JSON string into an object, then log a property from it.
challenge.starter_code:
const jsonText = '{"name": "Alex"}';
// Parse it and log the name

quiz.question: Which method converts a JSON string into a JavaScript object?
quiz.explanation: JSON.parse() reads a JSON-formatted string and returns a real JavaScript value.

content.explanation: A Promise represents a value that may not be ready yet, such as the result of a network request. Instead of blocking the program, code can attach a '.then()' callback that runs once the Promise resolves successfully.

examples.title: Using .then()
examples.explanation: Fetches data, converts the response to JSON, then logs the result once it's ready.

key_points: A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future
'.then(callback)' runs once the Promise resolves successfully
'fetch()' returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object

challenge.description: Write a fetch() call that chains a .then() to log the response.
challenge.starter_code: // Fetch data and log the response

quiz.question: What does fetch() return?
quiz.explanation: fetch() returns a Promise that eventually resolves to a Response object.

content.explanation: 'async' and 'await' provide a cleaner way to work with Promises, making asynchronous code read like ordinary step-by-step code. Marking a function 'async' allows using 'await' inside it to pause until a Promise resolves.

examples.title: Async Function
examples.explanation: Reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code, even though each 'await' step is asynchronous.

key_points: 'async' before a function allows using 'await' inside it
'await' pauses execution until the Promise resolves, without blocking the browser
async/await is often considered more readable than chains of .then()

challenge.title: Write an Async Function
challenge.description: Define an async function called loadData that awaits a fetch() call.
hints: Use await before fetch(...) and response.json()

quiz.question: What keyword must precede a function definition to allow 'await' inside it?
quiz.explanation: Only functions declared with 'async' can use the 'await' keyword inside them.

content.explanation: 'fetch()' is the standard browser function for making HTTP requests to APIs. Combined with async/await, it lets a page load real, live data from a server and display it dynamically.

examples.title: Fetching and Displaying Data
examples.explanation: Fetches a user's data and displays their name on the page.

key_points: fetch(url) sends an HTTP GET request by default
response.json() parses the response body as JSON
Fetched data can then update the DOM to display live content

rules.description: Must update textContent with the result

quiz.question: Which method parses a fetch Response body as JSON?
quiz.explanation: response.json() reads the response body and parses it as JSON, returning a Promise.

content.explanation: Network requests can fail, so it's important to handle errors gracefully. Wrapping 'await' calls in a 'try/catch' block lets a script catch failures (like a lost connection) and respond instead of crashing.

examples.title: Try/Catch with Fetch
examples.explanation: Catches and logs any error that occurs during the fetch, instead of letting the app crash.

key_points: 'try { ... }' contains code that might fail
'catch (error) { ... }' runs if anything inside try throws an error
try/catch is the standard way to handle failures in async/await code

challenge.title: Wrap a Fetch in try/catch
challenge.description: Write an async function that wraps an awaited fetch() call in a try/catch block.
hints: Wrap the await calls inside try { ... }

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a 'catch' block?
options: It runs before the try block
It runs code that might fail
It handles errors thrown inside the try block
It replaces the need for functions
quiz.explanation: The catch block runs only when an error is thrown somewhere inside the preceding try block.

content.explanation: Once a site is built, it needs hosting to be visible to the world. Static hosting services (like GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Vercel) serve HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files directly to visitors, usually for free for simple projects.

examples.title: Minimal Project Structure
examples.explanation: A typical minimal folder structure ready to be uploaded to a static host.

Static hosts serve pre-built files with no server-side code required
Most static hosts offer free hosting for personal and small projects

quiz.question: What is the conventional name for a site's default homepage file?
